new_en: Seif katan 1, "faithful." Those who say "faithful," etc., beforehand, meaning that they say, "Faithful to His covenant and steadfast in His word, Blessed are You, Hashem, who remembers the covenant," are mistaken, because it is explicit in the Gemara that this blessing does not conclude with a separate blessing formula. Here the text should read Shelah, because Shelah wrote this. What was printed as the word Shelah at the end of seif katan 2 is an error, for the Gemara explicitly states in Chagigah 16a: "Whoever does not have concern for the honor of his Creator, it would have been better for him not to have come into existence." The Gemara asks what this refers to, and R' Abba says: one who gazes at a rainbow. It further says there that R' Yehudah bar Nachmani, the interpreter of Reish Lakish, expounded: anyone who gazes at 3 things has his eyesight dimmed, including a rainbow, etc.

"And if the congregation prays early," etc. Terumat HaDeshen, siman 1, writes that in most communities the custom on long summer days is to recite the evening Shema and pray Maariv 3 or 4 hours before nightfall. They rely on Rashi, who holds that they fulfill the obligation through the Shema recited at bedtime. This custom spread because weakness descended upon the world and people desire to eat while it is still day. He concludes that even a Torah scholar, if he is in a congregation that prays and recites Shema early on long days and cannot separate himself from them, need not withdraw. He prays and recites with them and may rely on this. But if he is accustomed to other acts of piety, he should pray and recite Shema at the time established by the Sages according to all opinions. Mordechai likewise writes in the name of Ra'avyah that one who acts stringently and refuses to rely upon Rabbeinu Tam may appear presumptuous. Beit Yosef, however, writes that since according to several great authorities one does not fulfill the obligation through the synagogue reading, such stringency is not presumptuous.

In my view, the proper way for one who wishes to satisfy the matter is to rely upon Shema at bedtime, but to recite it then with intent to fulfill the mitzvah, not merely because of harmful forces. There is no need to recite all 3 paragraphs for the basic obligation if he already recited them in the synagogue, as Beit Yosef writes in the name of R' Yitzchak according to his approach. This is preferable to the approach of the Shulchan Aruch that one should repeat Shema after nightfall, for according to that approach it is very likely that one will forget to repeat it when the stars emerge, especially since he already recited Shema and believes that only a later repetition remains for publicizing the proper time. By contrast, at bedtime there is a natural prompt to recite Shema because of the established bedtime recitation, and a person is less likely to forget.

One might object that if he waits until bedtime he may eat, drink, and fall asleep before reciting Shema, like the concern expressed by the Sages when a person says, "I will eat a little," etc. But this cannot be decisive, because Tosafos did not raise such an objection against Rashi's view. It therefore appears that there is no special concern here, as Baer Heitev writes. Accordingly, one who wishes to act properly should recite Shema at bedtime with intent to fulfill the mitzvah. I later found in Mateh Moshe that Maharshal recited all 3 paragraphs at bedtime.

"One who urinates," etc. Even if he is clothed and urinates in front of his bed, the text speaks of one who is naked only because that is the ordinary case. [Rashi, Niddah 57a] Likewise, one who cuts his fingernails in their natural consecutive order brings himself to poverty, forgetfulness, and the burial of children. [Knesset HaGedolah] Rather, he should cut them in the alternate order recorded by the authorities, beginning with the left hand and afterward the right. [Hagahot Ashiri; Agudah; Beit David; Abudarham in the name of the sages of France and Provence]

7) There, "even if it is not on the fire, he is liable," etc. A kli rishon cooks even after it has been removed from the fire, for as long as its contents remain at yad soledet bo temperature, as stated below in siman 318, seif 9; see there.

"Further reduction." Meaning any food that a person is pleased to have dry out and further reduce. [Milchamot]

"That it is raw." This means that in such a case it may be placed there immediately before nightfall. But if he placed it there earlier in the day, it is forbidden, because it will already have cooked somewhat before Shabbos and he must remove it after dark unless it became fully cooked before Shabbos. See siman 254.

"That he covered the coals with ashes." It is unnecessary to cover them so thoroughly that no fire at all is visible. A minimal covering suffices. [Ran; Beit Yosef] Even if the coals later flare up again, it is permitted, because by initially covering them he demonstrated that he does not desire the coals.

"A raw piece." Placing 1 raw piece into the pot permits leaving the entire pot there, because he thereby puts the food out of his mind until the following day. This applies only when the piece is actually raw close to Shabbos.

"On top of it." The prohibition discussed by the Mechaber concerns leaving the pot on the stove where the heat is strong enough to create the concern that he may stir the coals. Placing it alongside is more lenient, as explained in the seif and in the authorities.

"Garuf and katum." Garuf means that the coals were removed; katum means that they were covered with ashes. The purpose is to weaken the fire and show that he has no interest in intensifying it.

"Fully cooked." Where the food is fully cooked and further reduction is detrimental, there is no concern that he will stir the coals. If further reduction improves it, the dispute stated by the Mechaber applies.

"Ma'achal ben Derusai." According to the lenient opinion, once the food has reached the stage of ma'achal ben Derusai it may be left on the stove even when the stove is not garuf or katum. Our custom follows this lenient opinion, as Rama states.

"An oven." Our ovens have the status of a kirah rather than the more stringent oven discussed by the Gemara, as the authorities explain.

"If he forgot." Where one left the pot there inadvertently, the food is permitted when it was fully cooked, even if further reduction improves it. If it had only begun to cook and was not fully cooked, it is forbidden until after Shabbos. If he left it deliberately in violation of the law, it is forbidden.

"A non-Jew returned it." Where a non-Jew returned the pot on Shabbos, its law is like one who forgot and left it. If a Jew returned it, its law is like one who deliberately left it. Where further reduction is detrimental, there is room for leniency because no benefit was obtained from the prohibited act.

"Directly upon the coals." All agree that actually insulating a pot in coals is forbidden. When the pot merely stands upon the fire and is uncovered above, some authorities do not regard this as hatmanah, and this is the custom. One should preferably loosen it somewhat from the fire before Shabbos so that it can be removed without moving the coals. If this was not done and the pot must be removed on Shabbos, a non-Jew should remove it if available. If no non-Jew is available, a Jew may remove it carefully, taking care not to stir or move the coals. If a slight movement occurs unintentionally, it is permitted because it was not intended.

Where coals are beneath the pot but the pot is not actually buried among them, removal is permitted when this can be done without stirring or arranging the coals. Where the coals surround the pot, however, Mordechai writes that a Jew should not remove it, because doing so necessarily moves the coals. The concern is not that he seeks to extinguish or kindle, but that removal itself will move them. See the related discussion in siman 254 and Tosafos, Yoma 44a.

"It is forbidden to use." Even for a use that does not require close examination, because one may come to tilt the lamp. See siman 275.

"It is permitted to use." Even if the lamps are standing in another room, because once there is a valid lamp somewhere else, he will remember and will not tilt even in the other places. [Ibid.]

"Without a lamp." For example, to draw wine from a cellar. [Ibid.]

"After the fact." It appears to me that if there is 1 valid lamp and beside it stands a lamp that is invalid for use, it is permitted to make use of the light. It is no worse than having only 1 lamp, as stated in siman 276. Although Bach is stringent here, he follows his own reasoning in siman 673, where he writes that a shamash does not permit use of the Chanukah lights. According to our ruling there, however, it is clearly permitted.
